name: Laser hair-growth helmet/cap

card.summary: Wearable low-level laser caps and helmets marketed for androgenetic alopecia; reviews report mixed-to-tentative benefit and call for larger trials.
card.aka: LLLT cap, laser helmet, photobiomodulation cap
card.price: About $2,000 for one premium helmet (forum post)
card.note: Several devices are FDA-cleared; long-term effects are unknown.

quick.overview:
Laser hair-growth helmets and caps are wearable devices using low-level laser therapy (LLLT) to treat androgenetic alopecia. Some are FDA-cleared, and prices vary widely; one forum user cited about $2,000 for a premium helmet.

Reviews summarised on Wikipedia range from little evidence (2012) to tentative benefit (2015, 2017), with authors calling for larger long-term double-blind trials.
quick.mechanism: Low-power red laser light is proposed to act on mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase in follicle cells. The mechanism remains under investigation.
quick.risks: Reported side effects are mild pain or skin irritation; long-term effects on skin and hair are unknown. Some devices call for eye protection.

lead: Laser hair-growth helmets and caps are wearable devices that apply low-level laser therapy (LLLT, also called photobiomodulation) to the scalp with the aim of treating androgenetic alopecia. Wikipedia lists hats, combs and helmets among home-use LLLT options. [1]

Reviews of laser therapy for hair loss are mixed: a 2012 review found little evidence, 2014 reviews were mixed, and 2015 and 2017 reviews reported tentative benefit, with 10 of 11 trials in the 2017 review showing improvement. [1] Reviewers have called for larger, long-term, double-blind trials. [1]
infobox: Up to about $2,000 for some helmets (forum report) [2]

paras: The main proposed mechanism involves the mitochondrial enzyme cytochrome c oxidase, and effects appear limited to certain wavelengths; effectiveness is still under investigation. [1]
Hungarian physician Endre Mester reported in 1967 that hair regrew faster in mice treated with a low-power laser, an observation made when a faulty laser was used in an experiment. [1]

No trials of specific helmet models were available for this article beyond summaries of reviews. A 2017 review reported 10 of 11 trials showed significant improvement in androgenetic alopecia versus baseline or controls; reviews suggested LLLT may work as well as or better than minoxidil and finasteride, but larger long-term double-blinded trials are needed. [1] Device type and treatment duration did not appear to change effectiveness. [1]
Reported side effects include mild pain or skin irritation; long-term effects are unknown and some devices require eye protection. [1]
On looksmax.org, users describe combining a laser helmet with finasteride and other measures. [2]

timeline.event: Mester reports faster hair regrowth in laser-treated mice. [1]

lore.intro: Laser helmets appear in forum hair-loss routines alongside finasteride and minoxidil. [2]

claims.claim: A laser helmet has a stronger regrowth effect than other treatments
claims.believers: One user reported denser hair after combining finasteride, a laser helmet and other measures, and said latest studies showed a stronger regrowth effect. [2]
claims.experts: Reviews describe mixed-to-tentative benefit and suggest LLLT may be comparable to minoxidil and finasteride, but call for larger trials. [1]
